title: Database Sharding — horizontal partitioning of data across multiple DB instances, shard key selection, cross-shard queries, resharding challenges.

s1_definition.profdef: Sharding is horizontal partitioning that splits a dataset across multiple database instances, each holding a disjoint subset of rows, so that total capacity and throughput scale beyond a single machine. A shard key determines which shard a row lives on; its choice governs load balance and query efficiency. Cross-shard queries and transactions are expensive and must be minimized, and resharding to add capacity is operationally challenging and must be planned for from the start.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has too many customers for one ledger book to hold. So it splits customers across several ledger books by a rule, say customers with account numbers ending 0 to 3 in book one, 4 to 6 in book two, and so on. Each book is smaller and faster to search, and clerks can work on different books in parallel. The rule for which book a customer goes in is the shard key. The trouble starts when a question needs data from all books at once, or when the bank must add a new book and reshuffle customers.
s1_definition.oneliner: Split rows across database instances by a shard key to scale beyond one machine, pick the key to balance load and keep queries single-shard, and plan for painful resharding.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sharding is horizontal partitioning that splits a dataset across multiple database instances, each holding a disjoint subset of rows, so that total capacity and throughput scale beyond a single machine. A shard key determines which shard a row lives on; its choice governs load balance and query efficiency. Cross-shard queries and transactions are expensive and must be minimized, and resharding to add capacity is operationally challenging and must be planned for from the start.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India has too many customers for one ledger book to hold. So it splits customers across several ledger books by a rule, say customers with account numbers ending 0 to 3 in book one, 4 to 6 in book two, and so on. Each book is smaller and faster to search, and clerks can work on different books in parallel. The rule for which book a customer goes in is the shard key. The trouble starts when a question needs data from all books at once, or when the bank must add a new book and reshuffle customers.

**One line to remember:** Split rows across database instances by a shard key to scale beyond one machine, pick the key to balance load and keep queries single-shard, and plan for painful resharding.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's single accounts database can no longer hold the growing customer base or sustain the write volume. The real problem is scaling writes and storage beyond one machine. This is exactly what horizontal sharding by account id provides.

Problem 2 — most operations, like reading a balance or transferring within an account, must stay fast and touch only one shard, while a rare regulatory report needs a total across all shards. The real problem is keeping common queries single-shard while still supporting the occasional cross-shard aggregate. This is exactly what good shard-key selection plus scatter-gather handle.

Problem 3 — the bank must add a shard as it grows without reshuffling nearly all accounts. The real problem is resharding safely. This is exactly what virtual shards and consistent hashing address.

We build a runnable sharding core: a `ShardRouter` that maps account ids to shards, several `Shard` instances holding balances, single-shard reads and transfers, a cross-shard scatter-gather total, and a resharding demonstration using virtual shards. The demo routes accounts, does a single-shard transfer, computes a cross-shard total, and adds a shard with minimal movement.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the sharding demo
java -cp target/db-sharding-1.0.0.jar com.bank.sharding.ShardingDemo

# Expected: each account routed to one physical shard; single-shard ops local;
# scatter-gather total across shards; adding db-3 reassigns only some virtual shards.
```

Note: the reassigned-count log compares virtual shard indices as Strings for the demo; in production the mapping and movement are tracked by a shard-management service.
sections.s5_journey:
The input is eight virtual shards over two physical shards, three accounts, a transfer, a cross-shard total, and the addition of a third physical shard.

Step 1: Each account id is hashed to a virtual shard, and the virtual shard maps to a physical shard. So each account lands on exactly one physical database instance, and the router logs which one, keeping routing deterministic.

Step 2: Balances are set and a transfer updates two accounts. When both accounts live on the same shard, the transfer is a fast local single-shard operation; if they lived on different shards, it would require a two-phase distributed transaction, which is why shard-key choice matters.

Step 3: The cross-shard total balance scatters a sum request to every shard and gathers the partial sums into a grand total. This works but touches all shards, illustrating why such queries are kept rare.

Step 4: A third physical shard is added, and the virtual shards are rebalanced across the three physical shards. Because the virtual-to-physical mapping only reassigns some virtual shards rather than rehashing every account, only a fraction of the data must move. The data that changed is the virtual-to-physical assignment for a minimal set of virtual shards.

```
2026-11-01 01:40:00 [INFO] SAV2001 on db-1
2026-11-01 01:40:00 [INFO] CUR3001 on db-2
2026-11-01 01:40:00 [INFO] Single-shard operations stay fast and local
2026-11-01 01:40:00 [INFO] Cross-shard total balance = 1300000
2026-11-01 01:40:00 [INFO] After adding db-3, virtual shards reassigned: 3/8 (minimal)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  account id → hash → virtual shard (0..7) → physical shard
    │ SAV2001 → v3 → db-1
    │ CUR3001 → v5 → db-2
    ▼
  single-shard read/write (fast, local)

  cross-shard total (scatter-gather)
    │ ask db-1.sum, db-2.sum
    ▼
  combine partials → grand total

  ADD db-3 (reshard)
    │ rebalance virtual shards across {db-1,db-2,db-3}
    │ only reassigned vshards' data moves
    ▼
  ~3/8 virtual shards move, rest stay (minimal migration)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sharding is horizontal partitioning that splits a dataset across multiple database instances, each holding a disjoint subset of rows, so capacity and write throughput scale beyond what a single machine can do. It is different from read replicas, which copy the whole dataset to scale reads only; sharding actually divides the data. At National Bank of India, the single accounts database eventually could not hold the growing customer base or sustain the write volume, and sharding by account id was how we scaled past that ceiling.

The single most important decision is the shard key, because it governs both load balance and query efficiency. A good key spreads data and load evenly and, crucially, keeps the common operations on one shard. For a bank, account id or customer id is a strong key because most operations, like reading a balance or transferring within an account, are naturally scoped to one account and therefore one shard. I avoid keys that create hotspots, such as a monotonically increasing timestamp, which would funnel all new writes to a single shard.

The main pain of sharding is cross-shard work. A query that must touch many shards, like summing balances across all customers for a regulatory report, has to scatter to every shard and gather the partial results, which is slow, and cross-shard transactions are worse because they need distributed-transaction protocols. So the whole design aims to keep the overwhelming majority of operations single-shard, and I accept scatter-gather only for the rare aggregates that genuinely need it.

The hardest operational challenge is resharding, because adding a shard with naive modulo hashing would remap almost all rows. I mitigate this with virtual shards, pre-creating many logical shards and simply reassigning them to new physical nodes, or with consistent hashing, so that adding capacity moves only a small fraction of the data. In the demo, adding a third physical shard reassigned only a few of the eight virtual shards rather than rehashing every account. The senior lesson I always stress is to plan sharding and choose the shard key before you desperately need it, because retrofitting a shard key onto a live banking system is one of the riskiest migrations there is.
